opus-5.5.text:
Well, the starting point for me is to look at how people and animals do it. When you walk from a sidewalk onto sand, or onto a slippery floor, or you pick up a heavy backpack, you don't stop and run some elaborate system identification procedure. Within a fraction of a second, within a few steps, your body has adjusted. You may not even consciously notice. That kind of fast, online adaptation is something biological systems are extraordinarily good at, and classical robotics has generally not been.

The traditional approach to legged locomotion was very model-based. You'd carefully characterize the robot's dynamics, model the contact with the ground, and design a controller around that. That works beautifully in the lab, on the terrain you modeled. But the real world doesn't cooperate. The friction changes, the ground is soft or uneven, the payload changes, the motors heat up and behave differently. So the controller is constantly operating outside the regime it was designed for.

With rapid motor adaptation, the idea was to make adaptation itself something the robot learns. We train entirely in simulation, but with a huge variety of conditions: different friction, terrain profiles, masses, motor strengths, and so on. In the first phase, the policy gets privileged access to these environment parameters, which we call extrinsics, compressed into a latent vector, and it learns to walk well given that information. Of course, in the real world the robot doesn't know the friction coefficient of the ground it's standing on. So in the second phase, we train an adaptation module that estimates that latent vector purely from the recent history of the robot's own states and actions. The insight is that the discrepancy between what you commanded and what actually happened tells you a lot about the world you're in. If your foot slides more than expected, that's informative. If your legs move more sluggishly, maybe you're carrying a load.

Then at deployment, the base policy runs at a high frequency, and the adaptation module runs alongside it, continuously updating its estimate of the extrinsics. So the robot is always adapting, not just once at the start. And the important thing is that it works zero-shot. We trained in simulation, put it on a relatively inexpensive commercial quadruped, and took it outdoors onto grass, sand, mud, hiking trails, oily surfaces, and it handled them without any fine-tuning in the real world.

Philosophically, I think this points to something more general. The distinction between learning and adaptation is really about time scales. Evolution and long-term learning give you a good prior, a good base policy, and then you need a fast mechanism on top that tunes it to the current situation. Rapid motor adaptation is one concrete instance of that, and I think the same principle will matter far beyond locomotion, for manipulation, and eventually for robots operating in our homes and everyday environments, where the conditions are always going to be a little different from anything they've seen before.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learned adaptation with classical model-based locomotion, but does not identify rapid motor adaptation as pursuing the same goal as classical adaptive control.

r002.rationale: It mentions adjustment within a fraction of a second or a few steps and continuous updating, but does not place adaptation on approximately a walking gait cycle timescale.

r003.rationale: It says the discrepancy between a command and what actually happens reveals the environment, with examples such as unexpected foot sliding and sluggish leg movement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about rapid motor adaptation starts from an observation about biology. When you or I walk from a carpeted room onto ice, or pick up a heavy backpack, we don't need to be retrained. We adjust within a few steps. Our bodies sense that something has changed, and the controller adapts. That's what we wanted for legged robots.

The classic difficulty is that the real world is enormously varied. Terrain can be sand, mud, grass, stairs, slippery rock. The robot's own body changes too, because motors heat up, payloads shift, and legs wear out. You can't anticipate all of that in a fixed controller, and you certainly can't collect real-world data for every possibility. So the question is how to get a policy that adapts on the fly.

Our approach was to train entirely in simulation, but with a twist. In simulation you have privileged information. You know the friction coefficient, the mass of the payload, the terrain height. So we first train a policy that takes in those extrinsic parameters explicitly, along with the usual proprioception. That policy learns to walk well across a huge randomized range of conditions, because it knows exactly what it's dealing with.

The problem, of course, is that in the real world you don't have access to those quantities. There's no friction sensor. So the second piece is what we call the adaptation module. It looks only at the recent history of the robot's own states and actions, roughly the last half second or so, and learns to estimate that extrinsics vector. The intuition is that the consequences of your actions tell you about the world. If you command a certain torque and the leg moves more than expected, that tells you something about the surface or the load. The adaptation module learns to read that signal.

Once you deploy, both pieces run together on the robot. The adaptation module continuously updates its estimate, and the base policy uses it. There's no fine-tuning in the real world, no reward signal, no human in the loop. The adaptation happens in a fraction of a second, which is why we called it rapid. And it was all run on a small onboard computer with just the joint encoders and an IMU, no cameras, no external sensing.

What I found compelling was how far this transferred. We took a quadruped out to beaches, hiking trails, construction sites, piles of debris, and it handled them without ever having seen real-world data. That gave me some confidence that the general recipe, learning a policy conditioned on latent world parameters plus learning to infer those parameters from experience, is a real principle and not just a trick for one robot.

I'd also say this connects to a broader view I hold about intelligence. Adaptation isn't a separate add-on module. It's intrinsic to how sensorimotor control should work. Perception and action feed into each other, and the agent is constantly estimating the state of itself and the world from the stream of its own interactions. We later extended this with vision, so the robot could look at upcoming terrain and plan footsteps, but the proprioceptive adaptation layer remained the foundation. You want the body to be robust first, and then vision gives you anticipation on top of that.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid adaptation and contrasts it with a fixed controller, but does not connect the learning-based approach to the same goal as classical adaptive control.

r002.rationale: It mentions adapting within a few steps and in a fraction of a second, but does not relate the adaptation timescale to a walking gait cycle.

r003.rationale: It explains that when a commanded torque produces more leg movement than expected, that mismatch reveals information about the surface or load and guides adaptation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is that you should not have to learn to walk all over again every time the ground changes. You want a policy that already knows how to walk, together with a mechanism that can adapt quickly to the conditions it encounters.

Imagine going from a hard surface onto sand. The friction is different, the ground gives way under your feet, and you have to adjust. For a robot, those properties are not necessarily known in advance. But their effects show up in the robot’s experience: it commands a movement, and the actual movement differs from what it expected.

So you can train in simulation across a range of conditions, and teach an adaptation mechanism to use the recent history of the robot’s motion and actions to infer what matters for control. That information then conditions the walking policy. At deployment, the robot can adjust as it moves, without having to retrain its policy for each new surface.

The interesting point is that it doesn’t necessarily need to identify the terrain by name. It needs to infer enough about how its body is interacting with the terrain to take the next step successfully.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning an adaptation mechanism for walking, but does not connect that goal to classical adaptive control.

r002.rationale: It says the robot adjusts as it moves, but gives no timescale tied to a walking gait cycle.

r003.rationale: It describes a mismatch between commanded and actual movement, but does not identify proprioceptively sensed bodily response as the signal for adapting locomotion.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a robot needs both a general walking policy and a way to adapt that policy to its current circumstances. The ground may be slippery or soft, there may be an unexpected slope, or the robot may be carrying a different load. You cannot anticipate every combination with a separate controller.

With rapid motor adaptation, you can train in simulation across a wide range of those conditions. During training, you give the walking policy information about the environment’s physical properties. Then you train an adaptation module to infer the information the policy needs from a short history of the robot’s movements and actions.

On the real robot, you don’t have access to all those physical parameters. But you do have feedback: you commanded a particular movement, and this is what actually happened. That discrepancy tells you something about the situation. The adaptation module uses that recent experience to adjust how the robot walks.

The interesting point is that you’re not learning to walk from scratch every time the terrain changes. You’ve learned how to adapt, so the adjustment can happen quickly while the robot is moving.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning to adapt walking, but does not identify this as pursuing the same goal as classical adaptive control.

r002.rationale: It says adjustments happen quickly while the robot is moving, but does not specify a timescale of approximately one walking gait cycle.

r003.rationale: It describes comparing a commanded movement with what happened, but does not identify the sensed response as proprioceptive.
